summary.text:
A £1.18bn debt book — £1,110.5m of it PWLB at a weighted 4.3% — set behind a strategy that says plainly what it is doing and why. Paragraph 53 pins internal borrowing at 'circa £80 million' and takes any new external as short-term (1–7 years) on the assumption those loans can be refinanced at lower rates when they mature. Paragraph 44 says the extra external the Council needs by 31 March 2031 is £928m, on a CFR that peaks at £1,699m in 2029/30 and comes with an Authorised Limit held constant at £1,714m across the five-year window. Every row of the §43 table ties on the identity CFR − external = shortfall; OLTL is inside the Authorised Limit (§62 mentions landfill aftercare) but not disclosed as a separate line.

The reconciliation is clean. We hold 172 PWLB loans for Cardiff, £1,108.03m at a weighted 4.34%, against their §19 print of £1,110.5m at 4.3% — £2.47m of drift on principal (0.22%) and one decimal place on the rate. What is worth writing about is the MUFG forecast the strategy was built on, dated 22 December 2025: 5yr PWLB to 4.60% by March 2026, 10yr 5.20%, 25yr 5.80%, 50yr 5.60%. On 14 August 2026 the certainty curve is 5.34% / 5.83% / 6.46% / 6.27% — every point 60–75bp above where MUFG said it would be by March, and 20–28bp above the paper's own 31 January snapshot. Bank Rate call was 3.25% by March 2027; SONIA today prices one-year Bank Rate at 4.11%. The dated bet has been contradicted by the market in the five months since.

Two smaller anchors. The 21 May 2026 LOBO call date on £18m has already passed and this paper does not tell us what happened; a mid-year report will. Break costs on our live book today are a net £112.3m discount, 123 loans below par against 46 above — the same shape as §58's historical read that penalties outweighed benefits, but on today's curve it is the reverse of true for most of the book. Indicative only; the DMO's quote is the only binding one, and no MRP or accounting treatment is modelled. No officer name or email is printed in this appendix.

contacts.note: No officer name or email in this appendix. §7 delegates to 'the Corporate Director of Resources, the S151 Officer' without naming them; §53 references 'the Council's Section 151 Officer'. Contact would need the covering report to the 5 March 2026 Council meeting.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy that went to Council on 5 March, ahead of the mid-year update that paragraph 4 says will come back to Council later in the year. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first. We hold 172 PWLB loans for Cardiff, £1,108.03m at a weighted 4.34%. That's your §19 PWLB line at 31 January — £1,110.5m at 4.3% — with £2.47m of drift and the rate rounding to yours to one decimal. So everything below is written against a book we can see clearly.

Paragraph 53 is where we wanted to write from. The stated position is 'a targeted level of internal borrowing would remain at circa £80 million' and 'any loans taken to meet the borrowing requirement are short term loans 1–7 years ... it is assumed they can be refinanced at lower interest rates when they mature'. Paragraph 52 says the same thing in the language of the market: rates are expected to fall over the next two years and long-dated borrowing now would lock in higher costs. That is a clear, dated bet, and paragraph 44 sets the scale — £928m of extra external borrowing to raise by 31 March 2031 on a CFR that peaks at £1,699m in 2029/30.

The reason to write is what the market has done since. The MUFG forecast the strategy is built on is dated 22 December 2025 (§31): 5yr PWLB to 4.60% by March 2026, 10yr 5.20%, 25yr 5.80%, 50yr 5.60%, Bank Rate to 3.25% by March 2027. Your own snapshot on 31 January had 5yr already at 5.06%, 10yr 5.63%, 25yr 6.21% and 50yr 5.99%. This afternoon on notice 314/26 the certainty curve is 5.34% / 5.83% / 6.46% / 6.27% — every point 60–75bp above where MUFG said it would be by March, and 20–28bp above your 31 January print. Bank Rate is still 3.75%, but SONIA prices one-year Bank Rate at 4.11%, not 3.25%. That doesn't mean the strategy was wrong; it means the anchor it was written against has moved, and 1–7 year borrowing on the assumption of lower refinancing rates is a decision that is effectively continuous once the roll starts.

Paragraph 44's £928m is a big number to write in that context. It works out to something like £186m of net new debt per year for five years, and once scheduled repayments are added back to gross it looks closer to £250m–£300m of gross new borrowing a year, most of it deliberately short. The other half of that picture is depth: July's sector lending was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%. The breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity, and we publish both daily fixings and the SONIA path so the roll can be watched against a curve rather than a quarterly forecast.

One dated question the paper leaves open. Paragraph 23 says the 21 May 2026 LOBO call on £18m — three £6m loans on a six-monthly option — was expected to be a live decision given rates. That date has passed at the time we're reading, and the strategy does not tell us what happened. A mid-year report will, and we'd be interested to see it.

While we were in the book we ran the DMO's premature repayment curve across all 169 live loans. Net position today, notice 314/26 PM, is a discount of about £112.3m: 123 loans below par against 46 above, with the largest single discounts on the 1.36%–1.93% coupons running to 2065–2071 and the largest premiums on the 7.13%–8.38% coupons maturing 2055–2057. Paragraph 58 records the historical review that 'penalties outweighed the benefits'; on the current curve that reads as true of part of the book and the reverse of true for the rest. To be clear on scope: we're not advising anything, we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment (both of which would matter for a decision), and only the DMO can give a binding quote. The point of running it is that it is a question that has a different answer on different days, and that answer is easier to keep half an eye on than to commission. Your book on the same curve is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

On the training side, five sit close to what the strategy commits to. Strategic PWLB borrowing goes straight to §53 and the £928m programme. Liquidity & cashflow forecasting matters given §54's own note that refinancing risk will increase substantially as more short-term borrowing is taken. HRA treasury & self-financing is worth the whole team's time given the £187m settlement buyout carrying 2% straight-line MRP and the HRA rate discount you qualify for. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator sits behind the discussion above. Working with treasury advisers is where the December MUFG forecast question best belongs. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 (Annex 4), Cardiff Council, 5 March 2026.
